content: In the 1960s and 1970s, pulmonary hemorrhage (PH) primarily occurred in full-term infants who had pre-existing illnesses, with an incidence rate of 1 to 3 cases per 1000 live births. Risk factors for PH during this time included the severity of the infant's illness, intrauterine growth restriction, the presence of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), coagulopathy, and the requirement for assisted ventilation. Currently, PH is observed in 3% to 5% of preterm infants who are on mechanical ventilation due to severe respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). These infants often have a PDA and have received surfactant therapy. The underlying cause of PH is believed to involve a rapid reduction in intrapulmonary pressure, which promotes left-to-right shunting across the PDA and leads to an increase in pulmonary blood flow. Retrospective case reports and one prospective uncontrolled study have suggested that surfactant therapy may yield promising outcomes in the treatment of PH. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of surfactant therapy, compared to either a placebo or no intervention, on mortality and other morbidities in neonates diagnosed with PH. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted on February 8, 2012, across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library (Issue 2, 2012), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, Controlled-trials.com, and proceedings from the Annual Meetings of the Pediatric Academic Societies (2000 to 2011). The Web of Science was also included in the search strategy. The selection criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that evaluated the effects of surfactant therapy in intubated neonates, either term or preterm (less than 37 weeks of gestation), diagnosed with PH. Infants up to 44 weeks' postmenstrual age were eligible for inclusion. The intervention of interest was the intratracheal administration of surfactant, whether natural or synthetic, at any dose, compared to either a placebo or no intervention. If relevant studies had been identified, the planned analyses would have included calculations of risk ratios, risk differences, and the number needed to treat to benefit or harm for dichotomous outcomes. For continuous outcomes, mean differences with 95% confidence intervals would have been reported. A fixed-effect model was intended for use in meta-analyses. The risk of bias in the included trials would have been assessed, and heterogeneity tests, including the I² statistic, would have been performed to determine the appropriateness of pooling the data. However, no randomized or quasi-randomized trials evaluating the effect of surfactant therapy in neonates with PH were identified. As a result, no conclusions could be drawn from such trials. Given the encouraging findings from studies with less rigorous designs, such as retrospective case reports and uncontrolled prospective studies, there is a clear need for further randomized controlled trials to evaluate the efficacy of surfactant therapy in the treatment of PH in neonates.
